newsitem.title: USA: Budget amendment urged to protect Social Security.
newsitem.headline: Budget amendment urged to protect Social Security.

text.p: Passage of a balanced budget constitutional amendment is the only way to guarantee the solvency of the Social Security system, Republican Rep. Bob Franks said Saturday.

Franks, a third-term congressman from New Jersey, was giving the Republican response to President Clinton's weekly radio address. He said claims by opponents of the balanced budget amendment that it would threaten the Social Security system were just scare tactics.
"That's outrageous, it's the worst form of demagoguery," Franks said.

"The truth is this vitally important program needs the protection of a balanced budget requirement. It's the only way to make sure Social Security stays solvent and can continue to send out the monthly checks seniors count on," he said.

The proposed constitutional amendment would require the government to balance its budget each year during peacetime and would make it harder for Congress to raise taxes, approve deficit spending or borrow more money.
The amendment needs a two-thirds majority vote in both the Republican-controlled House and Senate and ratification by 38 of the 50 states to become part of the Constitution.

The Senate has been debating the amendment since Feb. 5 and may vote on it next week when members return from a recess, but the outcome is too close to predict. The House is waiting for Senate action.
President Clinton opposes the amendment but cannot veto it. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan is also opposed.

On Thursday, Democratic Sen. Tim Johnson of South Dakota said he would vote against the measure because of concerns about Social Security. He cited a report from the non-partisan Congressional Research Service that questioned whether Social Security trust funds could be used to pay benefits in the next century when the huge baby-boom generation retires.
Franks said a permanently balanced federal budget would benefit all Americans by lowering interest rates on home mortgages and other loans.

"The choice is now clear. Either we tie the hands of Washington and stop them from spending our money or Washington will tie the hands of our children and continue spending them into debt," Franks said.
